article.scope_note: Scope reading. This article covers instruments whose primary output is the magnitude (total intensity) of the magnetic field, not its direction. It includes optically pumped alkali-vapour and helium-4 magnetometers operated as scalar instruments, proton-precession (PPM) and Overhauser instruments, and the laboratory and planned lunar devices that use the same physics. It excludes the generic magnetometer class (payload 012), fluxgate instruments that measure vector components (payload 013) and vector magnetometers (payload 014). Some instruments are vector-capable and also run in scalar mode, notably the Cassini Vector/Scalar Helium Magnetometer and the Swarm Absolute Scalar Magnetometer. They are included for their scalar function and cross-referenced to payload 014 for their vector function. The JPL optically pumped helium magnetometer for the lunar surface is included only as a proposal-stage cross-reference, because the source does not state a scalar mode. The Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometer is a fluxgate instrument and is discussed only as historical context. No flown or proposed lunar scalar magnetometer was confirmed in the sources reviewed.
article.overview:
A scalar magnetometer measures how strong the magnetic field is, as a single total-intensity value in nanotesla (nT) or gamma (1 gamma = 1 nT). It does not report which way the field points. Its output is one magnitude per sample. Many scalar sensors time a physical resonance: the frequency of a spin precession, or the frequency at which atoms respond to a radio or light field, is proportional to the field strength [7][11][10].

Scope reading. This article covers instruments whose primary output is the magnitude (total intensity) of the magnetic field, not its direction. It includes optically pumped alkali-vapour and helium-4 magnetometers operated as scalar instruments, proton-precession (PPM) and Overhauser instruments, and the laboratory and planned lunar devices that use the same physics. It excludes the generic magnetometer class (payload 012), fluxgate instruments that measure vector components (payload 013) and vector magnetometers (payload 014). Some instruments are vector-capable and also run in scalar mode, notably the Cassini Vector/Scalar Helium Magnetometer and the Swarm Absolute Scalar Magnetometer. They are included for their scalar function and cross-referenced to payload 014 for their vector function. The JPL optically pumped helium magnetometer for the lunar surface is included only as a proposal-stage cross-reference, because the source does not state a scalar mode. The Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometer is a fluxgate instrument and is discussed only as historical context. No flown or proposed lunar scalar magnetometer was confirmed in the sources reviewed.

Status categories used in this article: flown in space (Cassini, Ørsted, Swarm); prototype or test article, not flown (JPL lunar VHM); laboratory device (Allred 2002 potassium magnetometer); terrestrial commercial and observatory practice (PPM and Overhauser). Mission-status claims are given with their sources.

The Cassini plot above is a flight-data example of field magnitude crossing a magnetospheric boundary. It comes from the MAG instrument as a whole, not from a scalar-only sensor [6]. Its numeric axis has no unit label in the image or on the page.
article.description:
The scalar magnetometer family includes several physical methods. Each uses a different atomic or nuclear resonance, but all report |B|, the magnitude of the field vector:

- Proton precession magnetometers (PPM): a liquid sample rich in hydrogen protons is polarised by a coil current; the current is switched off, and the frequency of the protons' free precession is measured. A precision of up to about 1 part per million is described for these instruments [11].
- Overhauser magnetometers: a free-radical dopant in the same kind of liquid couples electron and proton spins. Saturating the electron resonance transfers polarisation to the protons, which raises the signal and reduces the power needed [11].
- Optically pumped alkali-vapour magnetometers: circularly polarised light aligns the spins of alkali atoms (rubidium, caesium or potassium). The field makes the spins precess, and the optical transmission changes with the precession, which gives the field magnitude [12][10].
- Optically pumped helium-4 magnetometers: a helium discharge puts He-4 atoms into a metastable state that can be pumped and read optically. ESA describes the Swarm ASM as based on electron spin resonance [7], and the JPL lunar VHM uses absorption at the helium 1083 nm line [13].

Spin-exchange collisions limit alkali-vapour sensitivity at normal atomic density and field. A 2002 laboratory result showed that operating at high potassium density and low magnetic field removes this limit [10]. This is the basis of the spin-exchange-relaxation-free (SERF) approach referred to in this family.

Scalar sensors report magnitude only. Vector instruments such as fluxgates (payload 013) and vector helium magnetometers (payload 014) report components. Some instruments combine both modes, as the Cassini MAG and Swarm ASM do [1][7].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose of a scalar magnetometer is an absolute reference for field strength. The Ørsted eoportal page describes its Overhauser instrument as the absolute reference for calibrating a boom-mounted vector fluxgate, with agreement better than 0.33 nT rms after calibration [9]. The Cassini V/SHM was built to measure the absolute magnitude alongside the fluxgate [1]; a secondary summary of the 2004 Cassini paper describes the scalar readings as used to calibrate the fluxgate data, but this was not verified in the primary text [2]. A scalar mode is therefore usually a calibration and reference tool, not a stand-alone direction-finding instrument.

For the Moon, the applications described in the JPL ARTEMIS-M poster are: (1) magnetic sounding to determine the internal electrical conductivity profile; (2) the effect of solar wind and the Earth's magnetotail on surface composition; (3) whether OH depletion in lunar swirls results from strong magnetic anomalies shielding the surface from the solar wind; and (4) the origin and history of the lunar crustal field [13]. These goals need long, stable records. The poster states a need for continual monitoring for more than one year, with accuracy below 100 pT at a 1 Hz cadence [13].

The Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometer, a fluxgate instrument, was designed for related goals, including the internal electromagnetic characteristics of the Moon and the interaction of the solar plasma with the surface [14]. A scalar sensor would add an absolute magnitude reference to such vector records, but no lunar scalar measurement was found in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle:
The Larmor relation links the precession frequency of a spin to the field. For a proton, the gyromagnetic ratio is 4257.60 Hz per gauss, so a 50,000 nT field (0.5 gauss, within the range of the Earth's surface field) gives a precession frequency of about 2.1 kHz. For a free electron, the value is 2.80246 MHz per gauss [11]. Scalar sensors measure this frequency and convert it to field units, so the reading depends on the field magnitude rather than its direction [11].

In a PPM, the sample is polarised along a coil that is perpendicular to the field, the polarising current is switched off, and the precession signal is induced in the coil and measured. Each cycle needs a polarisation step before measurement. The Overhauser method polarises the protons through electron-proton coupling, so measurement can run continuously and needs less power [11]. Vendor data quoted in a 1989 paper give 5 W of RF power for an Overhauser proton oscillator, compared with 100 to 200 W DC for a classical PPM [11].

In an optically pumped alkali or helium sensor, light and the magnetic field jointly determine the spin state of the gas. In a resonant mode, a radio field is tuned until it matches the Larmor frequency, and that frequency gives |B|. The Allred 2002 paper identifies spin-exchange collisions as the limit for alkali sensors at ordinary density and field, and shows that high density and low field remove that limit in the laboratory [10]. The 1962 Bloom paper addressed the design problems of rubidium optically pumped magnetometers, including amplitude variation with orientation and sensitivity in weak fields [12].

Orientation matters for resonance sensors. A scalar sensor can have a dead zone or null zone when the field is nearly perpendicular to the optical axis. A PDS catalogue summary reports a 45-degree half-angle null cone for the Cassini helium sensor, but this was not verified in the primary text [17][2].
article.scientific_importance:
Absolute field magnitude is a fundamental calibration quantity for magnetic science. It fixes the scale of vector measurements and is the basis for comparing data from different spacecraft and ground observatories. The Ørsted and Cassini examples both rely on this role [9][1].

For lunar science, the importance is the continuity of long-term, stable magnetic records. The JPL poster describes the need for a year or more of stable data to probe internal conductivity [13]. The Apollo LSM and the concurrent Explorer 35 orbital monitoring provided the lunar field data of that era [14]. A scalar record would add an absolute reference to such data, but the sources reviewed do not show that a lunar scalar record has been made.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a scalar magnetometer. Sensor species, cell or sensor-head volume, field range, sampling rate and operating mode all differ between designs, and the figures below belong to named instruments only. Where a value is not published in the sources read, the entry says so. The examples are arranged by status: flown in space first, then terrestrial and laboratory devices, then proposed lunar hardware.

examples.name: Cassini Vector/Scalar Helium Magnetometer (V/SHM) within the MAG instrument
examples.type: Flown planetary (Saturn mission); vector-capable instrument with a scalar mode
examples.status: Flown. NASA describes the V/SHM as used to make 'both vector (magnitude and direction) and scalar (magnitude only) measurements' [1]. Imperial College reports it stopped working after an Earth flyby (date not stated) [4]. Operating status at Saturn is therefore not resolved in the sources read.
examples.description:
The Cassini Dual Technique Magnetometer paired a fluxgate sensor (FGM) with the V/SHM. The NASA page gives the FGM as the vector sensor and the V/SHM as a vector and scalar helium sensor [1]. The V/SHM was provided by JPL and the FGM by Imperial College [1][4]. Cassini launched on 15 October 1997 [5].

Published operating values, as read: in scalar mode, the magnetometer measures fields in the range 256 to 16,384 nT, and the SHM is used only within about four planetary radii of Saturn where the field exceeds 256 nT [3]. For vector work the sensor covers two selectable ranges up to +/-256 nT [3]. The V/SHM sits at the end of the boom [3][4], which a PDS catalogue summary reports as 11 m long [17], not verified against the primary document.

Mass and power are given for the MAG instrument as a whole, not for the V/SHM alone: 3.00 kg and 3.10 W average operating power, both labelled 'current best estimate' [1]. V/SHM-specific mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources read.

Two claims could not be verified. First, a secondary summary reports the absolute accuracy as about 1 nT, and that Cassini was the first planetary mission to fly a scalar magnetometer. The primary Dougherty et al. (2004) text was not accessible, so both claims remain unconfirmed [2]. Second, the 45-degree null cone reported in a PDS catalogue summary [17] is unconfirmed.

The plot in the Overview is MAG data from Cassini's Saturn crossing [6]. It is not a V/SHM hardware image, and no V/SHM hardware photograph was verified.

examples.name: Ørsted Overhauser magnetometer (OVM)
examples.status: Flown. Launch 23 February 1999; regular operations halted in January 2014; end of life 30 June 2014 [9]. The eoportal page says that since 2005 the satellite measured only field intensity [9]. A SPASE record gives a different scalar span ending in 2009 [16]; the conflict is unresolved.
examples.description:
The Ørsted Overhauser magnetometer used the electron-proton coupling principle described above. The ESA eoportal page gives its measurement range as 16,000 to 64,000 nT at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with an absolute measurement error of less than 0.5 nT and an omnidirectionality deviation of less than 0.2 nT [9]. The instrument is mounted at the end of an 8 m deployable boom [9].

The OVM served as the absolute reference for a Compact Spherical Coil (CSC) triaxial fluxgate, which the same page gives a resolution below 0.25 nT and a dynamic range of +/-65,536 nT [9]. The page reports that after calibration the two instruments agree to better than 0.33 nT rms [9].

Mass and power are not stated on the eoportal page and are not publicly specified in the sources read.

The image below is a photograph of the OVM instrument, as captioned by eoportal. It shows a cylindrical sensor head with an electronics box on top. No dimensions are shown.

examples.name: Swarm Absolute Scalar Magnetometer (ASM)
examples.type: Flown Earth-orbit instrument (ESA Swarm constellation of three satellites)
examples.status: Flown. ESA describes two identical ASM sensors per satellite [7]. The launch date is not restated from a verified source in this run.
examples.description:
ESA's Earth Observation Gateway describes the ASM as based on the electron spin resonance principle, measuring total field strength, and states that it can also determine field components along three perpendicular axes [7]. The ESA page says two identical sensors are installed on the tip of the deployable boom, each with its own data processing unit [7].

ESA's page claims that the ASM makes 'absolute measurements without any drift or bias' and measures with greater accuracy than other magnetometers [7]. These are agency characterisations without numbers and should be read as claims, not measured performance.

A peer-reviewed in-flight paper (DOI 10.1186/s40623-015-0231-1) is reported, in a search summary only, to give an accuracy error of 65 pT (1 sigma) after Level 1b corrections against a 150 pT instrument budget, and a 250 Hz burst scalar mode alongside the 1 Hz standard output [8]. The full text was not read, so these numbers are unverified.

Mass, dimensions and power for the ASM are not stated on the ESA page and are not publicly specified in the sources read. The image is an ESA artist's view of the constellation and does not identify the ASM on the spacecraft [15].

examples.name: Terrestrial proton-precession and Overhauser instruments (ground and observatory practice)
examples.type: Commercial and observatory instruments; not space-flown in the sources read
examples.status: Ground practice. The figures come from a 1989 GEM Systems paper and describe the instruments of that date [11]. Current instrument specifications were not checked.
examples.description:
The 1989 GEM Systems paper gives a conventional PPM precision of up to 1 part per million, depending on polarising current, liquid and sensor volume [11]. It describes an Overhauser proton oscillator that needs 5 W of RF power, compared with 100 to 200 W DC for a classical PPM [11].

For a pulsed Overhauser magnetometer with a 0.15 litre sensor and a one-second measuring time, the paper reports noise of about 0.01 nT rms [11]. An airborne gradiometer built from a GSM-11A proton oscillator is reported to have noise below 0.05 nT at two readings per second, and about 0.1 nT at five readings per second [11]. The paper also gives an energy cost of about 1 watt-second per reading for a pulsed Overhauser instrument at 0.1 nT resolution, against 8 to 80 watt-seconds for classical PPMs [11].

The paper is written by a vendor. Its values are historical and instrument-specific, and they have not been checked against current datasheets. No mass or dimensions are given in the paper.

examples.name: Laboratory potassium spin-exchange-relaxation-free magnetometer (Allred et al., 2002)
examples.status: Laboratory only. The abstract read does not say whether the device reports total field or one component, so its inclusion here is provisional.
examples.description:
Allred, Lyman, Kornack and Romalis reported a potassium magnetometer operated at high potassium density and low magnetic field, which eliminates spin-exchange relaxation. The measured sensitivity was 10 fT per root hertz, limited by Johnson noise currents in the magnetic shields [10]. The authors estimate a shot-noise-limited sensitivity of about 2 x 10^-18 T per root hertz [10].

The result is a laboratory demonstration of the principle. It is not a flight instrument, and its size, mass, power and field range are not given in the abstract read.

examples.name: JPL optically pumped helium Vector Helium Magnetometer for the lunar surface (ARTEMIS-M)
examples.type: Prototype in a thermal enclosure; tested in a thermal-vacuum simulation; not flown; vector instrument with scalar mode not stated
examples.status: Prototype and test article. The poster says the work will make the system 'ready to propose as a stand-alone lunar instrument' [13]. Scalar operation is not stated; the cross-reference is to payload 014.
examples.description:
The JPL ARTEMIS-M task assessed magnetometer types for long-term lunar surface measurement and tested an optically pumped Vector Helium Magnetometer (VHM) in a thermally switched enclosure. The optical system uses a laser diode tuned to the helium 1083 nm absorption line [13].

The stated requirement is accuracy below 100 pT at 1 Hz cadence, stability below 25 pT, and continuous operation for more than one year [13]. The poster says that modelling shows two-sensor gradiometry on a 3 m boom can meet the requirement [13]. Thermal vacuum tests covered six day-night cycles [13]. The measured results are in figures that were not extracted, so they are not quoted here.

This is a vector instrument for payload 014 purposes. It is included only as a lunar cross-reference; no scalar-mode operation is described in the source.

key_values.status: prototype / test article; not flown; vector instrument (scalar mode not stated)

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No common dimensions apply across scalar designs. The stated geometry is in the example subsections: the Cassini V/SHM sits at the end of the MAG boom (reported as 11 m [17]), the Ørsted OVM sits at the end of an 8 m boom [9], and the Apollo-era lunar LSM booms were 100 cm long [14]. Sensor-head volumes are not published for most examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only published mass for a flown scalar-capable instrument is for the whole Cassini MAG instrument: 3.00 kg, current best estimate [1]. The V/SHM alone is not specified. The Ørsted OVM, Swarm ASM, JPL lunar VHM and terrestrial instruments have no published mass in the sources read. Mass values are therefore not comparable across the set.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Cassini MAG as a whole: 3.10 W average operating power, current best estimate [1]. Terrestrial Overhauser proton oscillator: 5 W RF, against 100 to 200 W DC for a classical PPM, from a 1989 vendor paper [11]. Pulsed Overhauser measurement: about 1 W-s per reading at 0.1 nT resolution [11]. Ørsted OVM, Swarm ASM and JPL lunar VHM: not publicly specified in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Scalar sensors have to work in the same environment as the vector instruments they support. The sources reviewed show the following requirements and operational evidence.

- Thermal control: the Apollo 16 LSM axes failed to flip on 24 July 1972, which the PDS document attributes presumably to elevated noon temperatures. On 3 March 1975 the z-axis data became intermittently static with off-scale low temperatures during the lunar night, and flip calibrations were stopped at night [14]. Thermal control had been improved for Apollo 15 and 16 after problems on Apollo 12 [14].
- Lunar thermal enclosure: the JPL VHM work built a thermally switched enclosure around the sensor to ride through the diurnal cycle, and the poster treats this as necessary for the one-year requirement [13].
- Field stability: the JPL lunar requirement is accuracy below 100 pT at 1 Hz and stability below 25 pT [13].
- Boom placement: the orbital examples use booms to place the sensor away from spacecraft fields. The Ørsted OVM is at the end of an 8 m boom [9], and the Swarm ASM is at the tip of a deployable boom [7].
- Planetary field range: in scalar mode the Cassini V/SHM is specified for 256 to 16,384 nT, and the SHM is used only within about four planetary radii of Saturn [3]. Radiation tolerance and lifetime are not stated for any example in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations:
A scalar magnetometer reports magnitude only. It cannot separate a field change caused by a direction change from one caused by a magnitude change. A vector sensor (payload 013 or 014) or a co-located pair is needed for direction.

Orientation-dependent dead zones are a known limitation for resonance sensors. The Cassini null cone quoted in a PDS catalogue summary is 45 degrees half-angle; this was not confirmed in the primary text [17][2].

Laboratory sensitivity does not carry over automatically to flight. The Allred 2002 result is a bench demonstration at high potassium density and low field [10]. Spin-exchange collisions limit ordinary alkali-vapour sensors [10].

Power and speed trade off. The vendor data show that the Overhauser method reduces power and increases speed, but these advantages are instrument-specific and dated [11].

Operating life and mode changes matter. The Ørsted satellite measured only field intensity after 2005, so its vector components were no longer measured after that year [9]. The Cassini V/SHM is described in the present tense by NASA but as having stopped after an Earth flyby by Imperial College; the scalar operating record at Saturn is therefore not settled [1][4].

No lunar scalar magnetometer has been flown in the sources reviewed, so the performance of scalar sensors in the lunar environment is untested. The JPL test results are in figures that were not extracted [13].

transportation_and_deployment.overview:
Transport and deployment depend on whether the scalar sensor is carried on a lander or rover, or in orbit. The Apollo-era surface magnetometer provides the only lunar deployment record reviewed, but that instrument was a fluxgate. The JPL poster sets the requirements for any future lunar scalar design [13][14].

No lunar lander or rover has been verified as compatible with a scalar magnetometer design. The compatibility statement below is therefore a general requirement, not a verified interface.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor head, boom, thermal enclosure and electronics into the spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth. The Ørsted satellite was photographed mounted for vibration tests [9].
Carry out pre-launch vibration and thermal testing of the integrated instrument. The eoportal caption records that the Ørsted satellite was tested this way [9].

Launch and transfer to the Moon or to a planetary orbit. For a lunar surface sensor, the JPL work considered the lunar thermal and diurnal environment, which applies after landing rather than during launch [13].

Deploy the boom and sensor head at the required distance from the lander or rover. The Apollo LSM had three orthogonal fluxgate heads on 100 cm booms, with sensors 70 to 75 cm above the surface [14]. The JPL modelling suggests that two sensors on a 3 m boom can meet the gradiometry requirement [13].
Commission the sensor, bring it to thermal equilibrium, and begin data collection. The Apollo LSM sent data at an average rate of 116 bits per second [14].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface: the Apollo LSM used a base box with legs, with booms set up by the astronauts, and sensors on gimbals so their axes could be flipped for calibration [14]. The JPL VHM design places a thermal enclosure on a boom, a candidate concept and not a flown design [13]. Orbit: the Ørsted OVM and Swarm ASM sit on deployable booms [9][7]. The Cassini V/SHM sits at the end of the spacecraft boom, reported as 11 m in a PDS catalogue summary but not verified against the primary text [17].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 16 LSM was deployed on 21 April 1972 and was turned off as part of the ALSEP shutdown on 30 September 1977 [14]. The Apollo 12, 15 and 16 LSMs formed a three-station network [14]. These are fluxgate instruments and are not scalar examples.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft was verified for any scalar magnetometer in this article. Any future lunar scalar design would need a verified interface definition covering power, data rate, thermal conditions and boom geometry before a compatibility claim could be made.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometer, flown on Apollo 12, 15 and 16, is the best-known lunar magnetometer. It was a triaxial fluxgate instrument with three ranges of plus or minus 50, 100 or 200 gamma, a resolution of 0.1 gamma and a 0 to 3 Hz frequency response. It had a mass of 8.9 kg and average power of 3.5 W in daytime and 9.4 W at night [14]. It is a fluxgate (payload 013) rather than a scalar instrument and is included only to show what was flown on the Moon.

The Apollo era also included orbital monitoring. The Explorer 35 magnetometers observed the lunar environment from lunar orbit while the LSM was operating [14]. The source does not state their scalar or vector configuration.

For scalar magnetometry, the historically important flights are Ørsted and Cassini. The Ørsted OVM supplied an absolute calibration reference for a vector fluxgate and was operated for about fifteen years [9]. The Cassini V/SHM is a scalar-capable helium sensor on a planetary mission. A claim that it was the first scalar magnetometer on a planetary mission is reported in a secondary summary but not verified [2]. The Swarm ASM extends the same approach to an ESA Earth-observation constellation [7].

For the Moon, no scalar magnetometer is known to have flown in the sources reviewed. The JPL ARTEMIS work is the most advanced lunar proposal in these sources, and it is a vector helium instrument [13].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
The main uncertainties and evidence gaps are listed here. Each one is also recorded in the data-quality notes of the JSON file.

- Cassini: the primary Dougherty et al. (2004) text was not accessible. The 1 nT accuracy and the 'first planetary scalar magnetometer' claim are unverified [2]. The 45-degree null cone and the 11 m boom come from a PDS catalogue snippet only [17]. The V/SHM's operating status after the Earth flyby is in conflict between NASA and Imperial College [1][4].
- Cassini mass and power are for the whole MAG instrument, not the V/SHM alone [1].
- Ørsted: mission-status conflict. eoportal gives operations halted January 2014 and end of life June 2014 [9]; a SPASE record gives a scalar span ending 2009 [16]. The eoportal page is dated 2012 but includes 2014 status text.
- Swarm ASM: accuracy and burst-mode figures come from a search summary of the 2015 paper, not its full text [8]. Mass, dimensions and power are not stated on the ESA page [7]. Launch date not restated.
- Terrestrial PPM and Overhauser figures come from a 1989 vendor paper and are not current datasheet values [11].
- Allred 2002 is read from the abstract only; the device's output mode (total field or component) is not stated in the abstract read [10].
- JPL lunar VHM: test results are in figures that were not extracted; the poster gives requirements and set-up, not measured numbers, in the text read [13].
- Lunar scalar magnetometers: no flown or proposed lunar scalar instrument was confirmed. Soviet lunar magnetometers (Luna 10, Lunokhod) were not verified in this run. MAVEN's magnetometers are described as fluxgates in a search summary, not checked against the MAVEN page; Tianwen-1 MOMAG's sensor type was not confirmed. A possible Mars Global Surveyor Overhauser sensor appeared in a garbled table and was not confirmed.
- Image rights: all images are reused under their publishers' terms, which were not separately verified. No image was checked at full resolution.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url and reference URLs in this file have query strings and fragments removed. The '?dl' parameter of the ESA Swarm source-file link was removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images. The Apollo LSM figure has no verified direct asset URL (image_url null); its PDF source page is linked instead.

data_quality_notes: Scope: the article covers total-field (scalar) instruments: optically pumped alkali and helium sensors run as scalar, proton-precession and Overhauser instruments, and laboratory and proposed lunar devices using the same physics. Generic class is payload 012, fluxgate is 013, vector is 014. Vector-capable instruments that also run in scalar mode (Cassini V/SHM, Swarm ASM) are included for their scalar function and cross-referenced to 014. The JPL lunar VHM is a cross-reference only, because no scalar mode is stated.

No flown or proposed lunar scalar magnetometer was confirmed in the sources reviewed. Soviet lunar magnetometers (Luna 10, Lunokhod) and any Mars Global Surveyor Overhauser sensor were not verified in this run.

Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometer (Apollo 12, 15, 16) is a triaxial fluxgate and is used as historical context only. Its values are taken from the PDS Apollo 16 LSM document (mass 8.9 kg; 3.5 W day and 9.4 W night; 116 bit/s). Secondary sources give conflicting power figures; the PDS values were used.

Cassini: the primary Dougherty et al. (2004) paper (DOI 10.1007/s11214-004-1432-2) redirected to a login and was not read. The approximately 1 nT absolute accuracy, the 'first planetary scalar magnetometer' claim and the calibration role of scalar data rest on secondary summaries and are unverified.

Cassini: status conflict. NASA's MAG page describes the V/SHM in the present tense as making vector and scalar measurements; Imperial College states it 'stopped working after the spacecraft's flyby of Earth' (no date). The scalar operating record at Saturn is unresolved.
Cassini: the 3.00 kg mass and 3.10 W power are for the whole MAG instrument (current best estimate), not the V/SHM. The V/SHM-specific values are not publicly specified in the sources read.

Cassini: the 11 m boom length and the 45-degree null cone come from a PDS catalogue search snippet only (reference 17). The scalar-mode range (256 to 16,384 nT) comes from a partial read of the Cassini MAG SIS (first 100,000 of about 232,000 characters); the appendix with scalar-data specifications was not reached.

Ørsted: eoportal gives operations halted January 2014 and end of life 30 June 2014, and states that from 2005 only field intensity was measured. A SPASE record (search snippet, reference 16) gives a scalar span ending 2009. The eoportal page is marked 'Last updated Jun 8, 2012' but contains 2014 text; the conflict is not resolved.
Ørsted: mass and power of the OVM are not stated in the eoportal page read. The 2003 Olsen et al. paper (Earth, Planets and Space) was identified but not read (Springer redirect), so it is not cited.

Swarm ASM: the ESA page gives qualitative claims only ('no drift or bias'; greater accuracy). The 65 pT (1 sigma) accuracy, the 150 pT budget and the 250 Hz burst mode come from a search summary of DOI 10.1186/s40623-015-0231-1, which was not read (Springer redirect). Authors and exact title of that paper are not confirmed. Mass, dimensions, power and launch date are not restated from a verified source.

Terrestrial PPM and Overhauser figures (precision 1 ppm; 5 W vs 100 to 200 W; 0.01 nT rms; 0.05 nT GSM-11A gradiometer noise; 1 Ws vs 8 to 80 Ws) come from a 1989 vendor (GEM Systems) workshop paper and are historical, instrument-specific values, not current datasheet specifications.

Allred et al. (2002, PRL 89, 130801): the abstract was read through an APS page summary; the full text was not read. The 10 fT per root hertz result is a laboratory result; whether the device reports total field or a component is not stated in the abstract read, so the example is provisional. Later SERF results were not verified and are not included.

JPL ARTEMIS-M poster (2022): text was extracted from the PDF. Requirements (below 100 pT at 1 Hz; below 25 pT stability; more than one year) and the 3 m gradiometer modelling statement are from the text. Thermal-vacuum results are in figures that were not extracted, so no measured performance is quoted. Scalar mode is not stated; the item is a prototype/test article, not flown.

Lunar environment: the Apollo LSM operational record (axis-flip failures at noon temperatures, static z-axis at night in 1975) is from the PDS document. No lunar thermal-vacuum or flight data for any scalar sensor were found.

Images: four direct image URLs were HTTP-checked (each returned 200 with an image content type): Photojournal PIA06348 (JPG), eoportal Ørsted OVM photo (Figure 7), eoportal Ørsted vibration-test photo (Figure 3), and the ESA Swarm artist's view (its '?dl' query string removed). The eoportal URLs were built from relative figure paths on the page and then checked. None was checked at full resolution. The Apollo LSM figure is embedded in a PDF and has no verified direct asset URL, so image_url is null and the PDF is linked.

Image content: the Cassini plot is a MAG data plot (top panel 'Magnetic field magnitude', numeric axis unlabelled); it is not a hardware photograph. The Swarm artist's view does not identify the ASM on the spacecraft. The Ørsted OVM photo was inspected and is consistent with its caption; the vibration-test photo was not inspected visually.
Image rights: reuse conditions for NASA, ESA and eoportal images, and the LETI credit on the OVM photo, were not separately verified. No image is marked public domain.

Research method: public web sources and the PDS and NASA archives were used. An internal Glean search was not run, since the facts requested are public instrument data; no internal EG context was added.
